title: Dominic and the Alibi
premise: Wendell Fairweather, archivist of St. Aldric's Cathedral, discovers a confession letter in the crypt mail slot postmarked the day after a parishioner's funeral — a letter claiming the funeral's celebrated 'sole witness' to a decade-old drowning never existed. As she traces the dead witness through parish registers, she realizes the letter was written by someone still alive and still afraid. The investigation collides with the cathedral's anniversary dinner, where the town's founding families gather to raise a glass, and Wendell must produce the 'dead' witness — a woman living under a borrowed name, kept hidden by the very archivist job Wendell inherited. In the end, Wendell chooses truth over the institution that employs her, unsealing the crypt's records at the dinner itself and forcing the town to bury its alibi alongside its dead.
about_author: Ines Iversen is the pen name of a former parish records volunteer who spent years alphabetizing other people's absences. She writes mysteries about quiet institutions and the documents that outlive the people they were meant to protect.

chapters.title: The Postmark Problem
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Sorting the cathedral's dead-letter tray, she finds a confession letter postmarked the day after Edmund Voss's funeral, claiming his celebrated witness never existed. She nearly files it — then notices the handwriting matches a 1994 baptismal register. Emotional beat: the itch of a record that refuses to stay alphabetized.

chapters.title: A Crypt with One Key
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She investigates the crypt's locked mail slot and learns only three keys exist: hers, the dean's, and one unaccounted for since 1994. The dean, Canon Pryce, warns her off with practiced warmth. Beat: unease beneath institutional politeness; the reader senses the archive itself is complicit.

chapters.title: The Drowning Year
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, with a flashback chapter of the 1994 drowning of young Tobias Marsh, told through clippings she reads. The official story: one witness, Edmund Voss, saw everything from the mill bridge. Beat: Wendell realizes the witness's testimony was the only thing that closed the case — and the only thing that opened a grave.

chapters.title: Alphabet of Absences
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She cross-references the letter's handwriting against parish records and finds a page razored out of the 1994 confirmation roll. Someone with archive access did this — before her time, or during it. Beat: paranoia; the archive she trusted becomes a crime scene.

chapters.title: The Widow's Second Grief
chapters.summary: Marian Voss's POV. Recently widowed, Marian receives an anonymous note: 'Ask Wendell about the letter.' She visits the cathedral, watching Wendell with an expression Wendell can't read. Beat: two women circling each other, each holding half a secret, neither sure the other is friend or threat.

chapters.title: Canon Pryce's Anniversary
chapters.summary: Pryce's POV. Preparations for the cathedral's 150th anniversary dinner consume him; he quietly reassigns Wendell's archive duties and requests the 1994 files 'for the commemorative exhibit.' Beat: menace dressed as ceremony; the reader sees Pryce managing the past like an event budget.

chapters.title: What the Mill Remembered
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She visits the ruined mill and finds a carved initials-and-date on the bridge stone matching neither Tobias nor Edmund. A local fisherman mentions a woman who 'used to watch the water' before disappearing around 1994. Beat: the first physical crack in the town's official memory.

chapters.title: The Letter Writer's Hand
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A retired graphologist confirms the confession letter was written by someone in their seventies now, left-handed, writing in a hand trained for liturgical script — someone raised in the cathedral's orbit. Beat: the suspect pool narrows to those Wendell sees every week.

chapters.title: Marian's Locked Room
chapters.summary: Marian's POV. Wendell confronts Marian; Marian reveals Edmund spent his last year terrified, burning papers, whispering about 'the girl under the stairs.' She gives Wendell his burned remnant: a corner reading '—ella.' Beat: grief and guilt braided together; the hunt gains a name fragment.

chapters.title: Ursula, Née Nobody
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She traces '—ella' through employment records of the cathedral school and finds Ursella Brant, a scullery maid who signed the 1994 register and vanishes from every document afterward — erased with the same razored precision. Beat: Wendell understands the erasure was professional. Archival work.

chapters.title: The Dean's Sermon
chapters.summary: Pryce's POV. At Sunday service, Pryce preaches on forgiveness and forgetting, eyes finding Wendell in the pew. Afterward he offers her a promotion to a distant diocese — a gilded removal. Beat: temptation and threat in one handshake; Wendell declines and feels the noose tighten.

chapters.title: Someone in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Working late, she hears the archive door and finds the 1994 box disturbed — her own notes gone. A figure escapes into the cloister; she glimpses a left hand, ink-stained. Beat: fear becomes personal; the archive is no longer safe, and neither is she.

chapters.title: The Witness Under the Stairs
chapters.summary: Ursella's POV, first appearance. In a coastal boarding house two towns over, an old woman who calls herself Mrs. Pell reads a newspaper notice of the anniversary dinner and begins packing a bag — and a gun she's never fired. Beat: the 'dead' witness lives, and is deciding whether to stay dead.

chapters.title: Two Funerals Deep
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She digs into Tobias Marsh's grave records and finds his body was exhumed and reburied in 1996, signed off by Pryce's predecessor — with Pryce as witnessing curate. Beat: the horror inverts; the case was never about who drowned, but what was buried twice.

chapters.title: The Confession, Complete
chapters.summary: Marian's POV. A second letter arrives for Marian: the confession's missing pages, naming Ursella as the true witness and Pryce's predecessor as the architect of her disappearance. Marian must choose between her husband's memory and the truth. Beat: Marian chooses truth, delivering the pages to Wendell.

chapters.title: Anniversary Eve
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. On the eve of the dinner, Pryce confronts Wendell with her own employment file — a fabricated incident designed to discredit her if she speaks. He offers her one last exit. Beat: the darkest hour; Wendell, alone, nearly takes it, then remembers Ursella's erased name.

chapters.title: Mrs. Pell Comes Home
chapters.summary: Ursella's POV. Ursella arrives in town the night before the dinner, visits Tobias's grave, and leaves a single white stone on it — witnessed by the fisherman from the mill, who sends word to Wendell. Beat: the dead witness walks back into the story that killed her.

chapters.title: The Glass Raised
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. At the anniversary dinner, as Pryce raises the commemorative toast, Wendell stands and reads the confession aloud. The room fractures; Pryce denies everything; then the doors open and Ursella enters. Beat: climax — truth spoken in the one room built on silence.

chapters.title: What Ursella Saw
chapters.summary: Ursella's POV. She testifies: Tobias's drowning was no accident — Pryce's predecessor struck him, and Edmund Voss, the 'sole witness,' perjured himself to protect the church that paid his debts. Beat: catharsis and horror; the town's founding families must hear what their glass toasted.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Pryce, complicit only in the cover-up's maintenance, resigns rather than face trial; Ursella, protected by her testimony, chooses to keep her new name — survival cost her the old one, and she won't pay twice. Beat: bittersweet justice; not every wound gets its name back.

chapters.title: Rebinding
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She restores the razored page to the 1994 register — a facsimile, with a note in her own hand documenting the erasure — and reopens the crypt's records to the town. Beat: the archivist's redemption; memory repaired honestly, scar tissue and all.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Wendell and Ursella's shared POV, alternating. Ursella mails Wendell a final letter: thanks, and a warning that every town keeps one more crypt. Wendell files it — then, on impulse, writes back. Beat: quiet resolution; the story ends with correspondence, not closure, and Wendell at peace with the alphabet of the living.
